source.title_on_document: AI models can predict and collaboratively modulate human memory search

supplement.holds: Detailed experimental and assignment procedures, model prompts, additional analyses, regression standard errors, and paired participant counts and tests.

paper_design_summary: The paper reports four online experiments on solo semantic fluency, next-word prediction, next-switch prediction, and human–human versus human–AI collaborative fluency, alongside archival human–AI benchmarks, a human–human timing pilot, and model-only prompt simulations (PDF pp. 18–19, 28–31, 67, 72). In the collaboration experiment, each participant worked with a human partner and an AI partner; AI prompt type varied between participants, while partner order and category were counterbalanced without an explicit statement of random assignment (p. 30). The collaboration analyses scored human concept production and semantic trajectories, while the prediction experiments compared unassisted humans with independently prompted LLMs (pp. 8, 11–14).

assignment.what_was_assigned: No AI-assistance allocation: all participants completed unassisted category fluency and retrospective switch marking; category order is not reported.
assignment.quote: Participants completed three rounds of the task, one for each of three categories: animals, clothes, and supermarket items.

arms.name: Solo human semantic fluency
arms.description: All participants completed the solo task in animals, clothes, and supermarket items (p. 28).

participants.exclusions: Before experiments involving typing, participants unable to type the test sentence in less than 15 seconds were excluded (PDF p. 31, Human participants). Solo and dyadic fluency sequences containing invalid category items or instruction violations were flagged by an LLM, manually inspected, and removed. Orthographic corrections were manually checked, and repeated items were removed after standardization (p. 32, Word Filtering and Standardization). Counts excluded by reason are not reported.
participants.who: Native English-speaking Prolific participants; 36 completed Experiment 1. Their solo sequences were pooled with sequences from Experiment 3, so the pooled sequence count is not an additional participant sample (pp. 18, 28–29).
participants.quote: 36 participants completed a web-based version of the semantic fluency task, where they were asked to name as many items from a category as possible within three minutes.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 18 and 28–29, recruitment and Experiment 1. PDF pp. 31–32, Human participants, Data Inclusion Criteria, and Word Filtering and Standardization (exclusions).

ai_tool.how_used: No AI assistance during the human task; these outputs subsequently supplied reference sequences for model and human prediction.

task.description: Name category members without repetition, then retrospectively mark starts of new groups of related items (pp. 28–29).
task.duration: Three minutes per category; three categories (p. 28).

assignment.what_was_assigned: A previously produced human word sequence was randomly assigned to each human predictor. This randomized the stimulus, not access to AI; all human predictors worked without AI assistance, and model predictions were generated separately.
assignment.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned one human sequence from one of the three categories.

arms.name: Human predictors
arms.description: Unassisted prediction of a randomly assigned sequence; 174 analyzed human predictors, with 58 per category (p. 29).

arms.name: Independent LLM predictors
arms.description: Models independently predicted the same human sequences; this is not a human treatment arm (p. 8).

participants.exclusions: Before experiments involving typing, participants unable to type the test sentence in less than 15 seconds were excluded (PDF p. 31, Human participants). The presented source fluency sequences were processed to remove invalid exemplars and spelling errors; typed predictions and target exemplars were standardized for matching (p. 29, Experiment 2). Solo and dyadic fluency sequences containing invalid category items or instruction violations were flagged by an LLM, manually inspected, and removed. Orthographic corrections were manually checked, and repeated items were removed after standardization (p. 32, Word Filtering and Standardization). This list filtering describes the source fluency sequences, not exclusion of incorrect predictions. Counts excluded by reason are not reported.
participants.who: Native English-speaking Prolific participants. The paper gives 174 human predictors in the analytic dataset, not a separate pre-exclusion randomized total (pp. 18, 29).
participants.quote: Data from 174 human participants (58 per category) were collected in the next-exemplar prediction task.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 18 and 29, recruitment and Experiment 2. PDF pp. 31–32, Human participants, Data Inclusion Criteria, and Word Filtering and Standardization (exclusions).

ai_tool.name_model: Gemini-3-Pro; Llama-3.3 70B-Instruct in a supplementary comparison
ai_tool.how_used: LLMs independently predicted the next human category member using theory-driven cognitive prompts; no model predictions were supplied as assistance to the human predictors (p. 8; p. 30, model-choice note).

task.description: Predict the next word in another person’s solo semantic-fluency sequence, receiving feedback on correct predictions (p. 29).

outcomes.name: Next-word prediction accuracy
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Proportion of correctly predicted next exemplars, summarized at the human participant–sequence assignment level and paired with independent Gemini-3-Pro predictions for the same sequence (PDF pp. 7–8, Figure 3; p. 29, Experiment 2). Typed predictions and target exemplars were standardized for matching. Human predictors received immediate correctness feedback but no AI predictions or assistance. Category and sequence-position analyses are variants of the same accuracy outcome; Figure S7 (p. 65) repeats the benchmark with Llama-3.3 70B-Instruct.

contrasts.reported: Independent Gemini-3-Pro predictions versus unassisted human predictors: AI M = 0.138, 95% CI [0.128, 0.149] vs. human M = 0.079, 95% CI [0.071, 0.088]; absolute advantage = +5.91 percentage points; two-sided paired Wilcoxon W = 936.5, p < 0.0001, n = 174. This is prediction accuracy, not an effect of AI assistance on human creative output.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8, Cognitive Micro-Alignment, overall comparison associated with Figure 3B.

assignment.what_was_assigned: A previously produced human sequence was randomly assigned for switch prediction. This was random stimulus assignment, not random assignment of AI assistance; the solo task preceded the prediction block.
assignment.quote: Sequences were randomly assigned and presented to participants as described in Experiment 2.

arms.name: Human solo fluency and switch prediction
arms.description: Unassisted human task. The paper reports 181 prediction sessions and separately identifies 92 people contributing solo sequences; a unique-person total for the entire experiment is not stated (p. 29).

arms.name: Independent LLM switch prediction
arms.description: LLM predictions were compared with human predictions on the same sequences; no human received model assistance (pp. 8, 26–27).

participants.exclusions: Before experiments involving typing, participants unable to type the test sentence in less than 15 seconds were excluded (PDF p. 31, Human participants). Solo and dyadic fluency sequences containing invalid category items or instruction violations were flagged by an LLM, manually inspected, and removed. Orthographic corrections were manually checked, and repeated items were removed after standardization (p. 32, Word Filtering and Standardization). The solo block followed Experiment 1 and sequence presentation followed Experiment 2 (p. 29, Experiment 3). Counts excluded by reason are not reported.
participants.who: Native English-speaking Prolific participants. The switch analysis counts 181 sessions, not explicitly unique people; 92 participants are separately reported as contributing solo sequences. Neither 181 nor the pooled 190 solo sequences is entered as the study-wide people count (pp. 18–19, 29).
participants.quote: The next-switch prediction analysis included 181 sessions (62 animals, 59 clothes, and 60 supermarket items).
participants.locator: PDF pp. 18–19 and 29, recruitment, solo-sequence pooling, and Experiment 3. PDF pp. 31–32, Human participants, Data Inclusion Criteria, and Word Filtering and Standardization (exclusions).

ai_tool.how_used: Models independently predicted whether the next word would switch semantic subcategory; their predictions were compared against unassisted human predictions (pp. 8, 26–27).

task.description: Complete a solo semantic-fluency block, predict switches in another person’s sequence, then mark switches and label clusters (p. 29).
task.duration: The solo fluency block follows the three-minute task described for Experiment 1; duration of later blocks is not stated (pp. 28–29).

assignment.what_was_assigned: AI prompt type (convergent, divergent, inferred) varied between participants. Human versus AI partner varied within participants. Partner order and the animals/clothes category assignment were counterbalanced; the text does not state random assignment of either prompt type or condition order. Design is coded other because randomization is unconfirmed, not because non-random allocation is established.
assignment.quote: To control for sequence effects, the order of the dyad types and the assignment of the two distinct categories (“animals” and “clothes”) were counterbalanced across participants.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 30, Supplementary Methods, Experiment 4 and LLM partners.

arms.name: Human–human
arms.description: Human partner with alternating turns. The full valid condition includes 192 people in 96 dyads; 129 people also had valid human–AI data and entered paired analyses (pp. 11, 30, 71).

arms.name: Human–AI: convergent
arms.description: Llama supplies a word in the human’s current semantic subcategory. There are 48 valid human–AI dyads, each containing one human; 45 people entered paired analyses (pp. 11, 30, 71).

arms.name: Human–AI: divergent
arms.description: Llama supplies a word outside the human’s current semantic subcategory. There are 46 valid human–AI dyads, each containing one human; 36 people entered paired analyses (pp. 11, 30, 71).

arms.name: Human–AI: inferred
arms.description: Llama is instructed to help maximize valid category words without a specified convergence/divergence strategy. There are 50 valid human–AI dyads, each containing one human; 48 people entered paired analyses (pp. 11, 30, 71).

participants.exclusions: Before experiments involving typing, participants unable to type the test sentence in less than 15 seconds were excluded (PDF p. 31, Human participants). Solo and dyadic fluency sequences containing invalid category items or instruction violations were flagged by an LLM, manually inspected, and removed. Orthographic corrections were manually checked, and repeated items were removed after standardization (p. 32, Word Filtering and Standardization). For collaborative word-count analyses, participants completing at least one dyadic task were included. Human-dyad analyses excluded participants whose partner submitted no words or who returned their Prolific submission. Within-person comparisons required completion of both dyadic tasks (p. 31, Data Inclusion Criteria). Counts excluded by reason are not reported; no randomized total is inferred.
participants.who: Native English-speaking Prolific participants. The initial pool was 207; full valid condition-specific samples were 192 people with human partners and 144 with AI partners, overlapping in 129 people who entered paired analyses. Arm counts describe the full valid conditions and must not be summed. The overall distinct-person total after filtering across all conditions is not explicitly printed and is therefore left null; the explicitly reported paired subset establishes that at least 129 people were analyzed (pp. 11, 18–19, 30–31, 71).
participants.quote: 129 participants were included in the paired analyses, of which 48 completed dyadic SFT with inferred prompts, 36 with divergent prompts and 45 with convergent prompts.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 11 and 30–31, sample and inclusion rules; p. 18, recruitment; p. 71, Figure S12, paired sample. PDF pp. 31–32, Human participants, Data Inclusion Criteria, and Word Filtering and Standardization (exclusions).

ai_tool.how_used: A concealed AI partner supplies one category word on alternating turns. Convergent, divergent, or inferred prompts guide its behavior; it receives the updated human word list. Model responses are delayed to approximate human response timing (pp. 11, 30–31).

task.description: Collaboratively produce as many nonrepeating animals or clothing items as possible, once with a human and once with an AI partner; participants were not told their partner’s identity (pp. 29–30).
task.duration: Two tasks of three minutes each (p. 30).

outcomes.name: Individual human concept production
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of unique valid concepts produced by the individual human participant during the alternating collaborative task; excludes the partner’s contributions from that participant’s score (PDF p. 14, Figure 5D; concept counting and filtering, pp. 11 and 32). Human–AI trials provided AI-generated partner words during production; human–human trials provided a human partner. The pooled comparison combines prompt types and the animals/clothes categories. Figure S12B separately reports paired individual counts for people with valid data in both partner conditions (p. 71).

contrasts.reported: Human–AI versus human–human, pooled across prompt types and the animals/clothes categories: the number of concepts produced by the individual human partner did not differ; Mann–Whitney U = 1.45 × 10^4, p = 0.44. Figure 5D reports the overall condition comparison; the separately reported 129-person subset applies to the paired analyses in Figure S12.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 14, Figure 5D and caption; p. 11, definition of the semantic-fluency score.

contrasts.control_arm: Human–human (same participants in the convergent subgroup)
contrasts.reported: Within-person comparison of individual human word counts: two-tailed paired t-test, t = 0.540, p = 0.708 (Holm–Bonferroni corrected), n = 45 people completing both conditions. The paired analyses include 129 people in total across prompt groups. This is separate from the pooled Mann–Whitney comparison in Figure 5D.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 71, Figure S12B and final paired-sample sentence.

contrasts.control_arm: Human–human (same participants in the divergent subgroup)
contrasts.reported: Within-person comparison of individual human word counts: two-tailed paired t-test, t = 1.938, p = 0.182 (Holm–Bonferroni corrected), n = 36 people completing both conditions. The paired analyses include 129 people in total across prompt groups. This is separate from the pooled Mann–Whitney comparison in Figure 5D.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 71, Figure S12B and final paired-sample sentence.

contrasts.control_arm: Human–human (same participants in the inferred subgroup)
contrasts.reported: Within-person comparison of individual human word counts: two-tailed paired t-test, t = 0.936, p = 0.708 (Holm–Bonferroni corrected), n = 48 people completing both conditions. The paired analyses include 129 people in total across prompt groups. This is separate from the pooled Mann–Whitney comparison in Figure 5D.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 71, Figure S12B and final paired-sample sentence.

outcomes.name: Change in similarity to one’s own preceding word, late minus early phase
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: ConceptNet cosine similarity between a human-produced word and the same human’s preceding word, summarized as the mean late-minus-early phase change after a median split by total word count (PDF pp. 12, 25–26 and 74, Figure S15A). AI was available in the human–AI condition; the comparator used a human partner. SEMs are retained as SEMs of the arm-specific phase changes. Figures 5B and S15A also compare with independently collected solo sequences. Figure S11 (p. 70) reports self-versus-partner similarity distributions by prompt and category; Figure S14 (p. 73) examines preceding-word similarity by switch/non-switch status. Figure S16B (p. 75) breaks the self-similarity change down by AI prompt: inferred −0.063 ± 0.014 SEM, p = 6.36 × 10^-6; convergent −0.064 ± 0.015 SEM, p = 8.57 × 10^-5; divergent −0.073 ± 0.015 SEM, p = 6.98 × 10^-6 (two-sided one-sample Wilcoxon tests against zero). No prompt-pair comparison reached significance (all p_corrected > 0.39, Holm–Bonferroni). These semantic relations are within a person’s sequence or dyad, not across independent participants’ outputs.

contrasts.reported: Mean change in self-similarity (late minus early): Human–AI −0.067 ± 0.008 SEM versus Human–Human −0.044 ± 0.008 SEM; Mann–Whitney U = 1.57 × 10^4, p = 3.63 × 10^-2 uncorrected, p_corrected = 7.27 × 10^-2 (Holm–Bonferroni), not significant after correction. This measures semantic movement within a person’s sequence, not homogenization across different people.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 74, Figure S15A and caption; p. 14, Figure 5B.

outcomes.name: Dyad-level unique-concept production
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of unique valid concepts in the complete alternating dyad sequence, including contributions from both partners. This differs from individual human production in S4-O1 (PDF pp. 11 and 14). Per-arm n values count dyads; no combined n_units is inferred. The nominal comparison counts the union of concepts from each constructed pair of independently produced solo sequences; n = 3,846 counts constructed pairs, not people (pp. 11 and 71, Figure S12A). Category-specific versions appear in Figure S9 (p. 68).

contrasts.reported: Unique concepts per dyad, pooled across animals and clothes: human–human n = 96 dyads, median = 33.0 [IQR: 28.8, 39.0]; human–AI convergent n = 48 dyads, median = 34.0 [IQR: 30.0, 38.2]; divergent n = 46 dyads, median = 31.5 [IQR: 27.2, 36.8]; inferred n = 50 dyads, median = 34.0 [IQR: 29.0, 40.0]. The text reports no significant overall human–AI versus human–human differences. Numerical direct-comparison test statistics are not supplied here; the printed U statistics in Figure S12A instead compare each dyad condition with nominal pairs.
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Dyadic Experiments; p. 71, Figure S12A. Arm summaries are medians/IQRs and counts, not means/SDs. The none availability code concerns the listed inferential-statistic categories for this direct comparison.

contrasts.control_arm: Nominal pairs of independently produced solo human sequences
contrasts.reported: Human–AI convergent: n = 48 dyads, median = 34.0 [IQR: 30.0, 38.2]; nominal reference: n = 3,846 constructed pairs, median = 59.0 [IQR: 51.0, 66.0]; Mann–Whitney U = 180,267, p < 0.001. Figure S12A specifies Holm–Bonferroni correction. The nominal pairs reuse solo sequences and are not independent people or an assigned control arm.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11, Dyadic Experiments; p. 71, Figure S12A.

contrasts.control_arm: Nominal pairs of independently produced solo human sequences
contrasts.reported: Human–AI divergent: n = 46 dyads, median = 31.5 [IQR: 27.2, 36.8]; nominal reference: n = 3,846 constructed pairs, median = 59.0 [IQR: 51.0, 66.0]; Mann–Whitney U = 173,486.5, p < 0.001. Figure S12A specifies Holm–Bonferroni correction. The nominal pairs reuse solo sequences and are not independent people or an assigned control arm.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11, Dyadic Experiments; p. 71, Figure S12A.

contrasts.control_arm: Nominal pairs of independently produced solo human sequences
contrasts.reported: Human–AI inferred: n = 50 dyads, median = 34.0 [IQR: 29.0, 40.0]; nominal reference: n = 3,846 constructed pairs, median = 59.0 [IQR: 51.0, 66.0]; Mann–Whitney U = 185,744, p < 0.001. Figure S12A specifies Holm–Bonferroni correction. The nominal pairs reuse solo sequences and are not independent people or an assigned control arm.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11, Dyadic Experiments; p. 71, Figure S12A.

outcomes.name: Change in similarity to the partner’s preceding word, late minus early phase
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: ConceptNet cosine similarity between each human word and the immediately preceding partner word, averaged within early and late task phases defined by a median split of word count, then expressed as late minus early (PDF pp. 12, 25–26 and 74, Figure S15B). AI was available in the human–AI condition; the comparator used a human partner. SEMs describe the arm-specific mean phase changes. Figure S11 (p. 70) also reports self-versus-other similarity distributions by prompt and category. Figure S14 (p. 73) separates similarity to the preceding word by category and by switch/non-switch status, using the sequence-specific median cosine-similarity threshold. These are within-sequence or within-dyad relations, not homogenization across independent participants.

contrasts.reported: Mean change in similarity to the partner’s previous word (late minus early): human–AI −0.038 ± 0.007 SEM versus human–human −0.062 ± 0.007 SEM. Two-sided Mann–Whitney U = 1.22 × 10^4, p_corrected = 5.97 × 10^-2 (Holm–Bonferroni); no significant between-condition difference. The ± values are SEMs, not SDs or an SE for the between-condition contrast.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 74, Figure S15B and caption.

outcomes.name: Partner-word similarity to the human semantic-transition midpoint
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: For each human–partner–human triplet, compute the midpoint in embedding space between the human’s words before and after the partner turn, then compare the intervening partner word with that midpoint using cosine similarity (PDF pp. 13–14, Figure 5C; ConceptNet embedding method, pp. 25–26). This scores within-dyad semantic geometry. The caption does not explicitly state whether the tests aggregate triplet scores per person, so the analysis unit and n_units are left null. AI was present for the human–AI sequences and absent for human–human sequences.

contrasts.reported: AI-partner words had higher mean cosine similarity to the human semantic-transition midpoint: Mann–Whitney U = 8.94 × 10^3, p = 2.93 × 10^-8. Similarity variance was also higher: Brown-Forsythe W = 44.72, p = 9.6 × 10^-11; HA SD = 0.124 versus HH SD = 0.068. Numerical arm means are not printed. Figure error bars are SEMs; the printed 0.124 and 0.068 values are SDs.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 14, Figure 5C and caption; p. 13, semantic-midpoint definition.

studies.label: Archival human-sequence benchmarks and model alignment analyses

assignment.what_was_assigned: Previously collected unassisted human sequences were compared with model-generated sequences and used as model contexts; people were not assigned to AI assistance. Prefix/shuffle and prompting manipulations operated on model inputs.
assignment.quote: We use one of the currently most capable frontier reasoning LLMs (Gemini-3-Pro) to generate SFT sequences and compare them with a set of n = 141 human-generated animal sequences from an earlier study [21].
assignment.locator: PDF pp. 6 and 10, Cognitive Macro-Alignment and Cognitive Micro-Alignment.

arms.name: Archived human solo outputs
arms.description: Existing human animal-name sequences used as references and model contexts (pp. 6, 10, 31).

arms.name: LLM sequences and predictions
arms.description: Independent model generation, context manipulations, and prompt comparisons using human sequence references (pp. 6, 10, 33–34).

participants.who: Previously collected human fluency data, with 141 sequences in the macro-alignment benchmark and 699 trajectories in the context-sensitivity analyses, of which 648 were complete across controls. These are reported as sequences/trajectories, so a unique analyzed-people count is left null; demographic composition is not stated here (pp. 6, 10, 31).
participants.quote: on 699 human “animals” semantic foraging trajectories [21, 42], with paired Figure 4B–C analyses restricted to the 648 sequences complete across all control conditions.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 6 and 10, archival sequence counts; p. 31, Additional Data.

ai_tool.name_model: Gemini 2.5 and 3 models; Llama-3.3 70B-Instruct for perplexity
ai_tool.how_used: Models independently generate category sequences or predict human continuations; an open-weight model supplies token probabilities for perplexity. Humans do not receive assistance in these benchmarks (pp. 6, 10, 17, 30).

task.description: Analyze archived solo animal-name fluency sequences and corresponding model generations, including sequence similarity, semantic geometry, and sensitivity to context (pp. 6, 10).

outcomes.name: BLEU overlap with human reference sequences
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The reported reference corpus contains 141 archived human animal-name sequences (PDF p. 6); n_units records that human-sequence count, not unique people or a summed human-plus-model output total. Humans generated their sequences without AI assistance; model outputs were generated separately. Candidate-sequence overlap with a human reference set is measured using clipped unigram, bigram, and trigram precision and a brevity penalty (PDF p. 26, BLEU score details). The comparison is model-to-human-reference versus human-to-human-reference similarity, not an effect of AI assistance.

contrasts.reported: Human-to-human BLEU M = 0.326, 95% CI [0.304, 0.347]; Gemini-3-Pro-to-human BLEU M = 0.626, CI [0.615, 0.637]. Higher raw BLEU means greater overlap; direction is coded treatment_lower on the codebook’s diversity orientation. No standardized or derived effect is calculated.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6, Cognitive Macro-Alignment and Figure 2C; p. 5, Figure 2 caption.

diversity_detail.metric: BLEU n-gram overlap; higher raw scores indicate greater similarity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each human or independently model-generated candidate sequence is compared with a set of human reference sequences. The archival reference corpus contains 141 human animal-name sequences (PDF p. 6); BLEU computation is described on p. 26.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Confidence intervals are printed on PDF p. 6; their construction is not specified there. Figure 2C (p. 5) reports one-sided paired Wilcoxon tests between adjacent models/comparators, without a direct Gemini-3-Pro-versus-human test statistic.
diversity_detail.notes: Question none: this is an AI-versus-human output benchmark, not AI-assisted human production. The direction field reverses the similarity orientation for diversity; the raw BLEU values are retained. Overlap with human references does not by itself measure dispersion among independent AI-assisted participants.

outcomes.name: Semantic-trajectory spectral gap
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The reported reference corpus contains 141 archived human animal-name sequences (PDF p. 6); n_units records that human-sequence count, not unique people or a summed human-plus-model output total. Humans generated their sequences without AI assistance; model outputs were generated separately. Difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues of the within-trajectory cosine-similarity matrix of ConceptNet embeddings. A larger gap indicates greater dominance of one semantic axis (PDF pp. 6 and 32). This characterizes one sequence’s geometry, not between-person homogenization.

contrasts.reported: Gemini-3-Pro M = 5.779, CI [5.639, 5.911]; human 4.878, CI [4.736, 5.020]. Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.0001; a numerical W statistic is not printed for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7, continuation of Cognitive Macro-Alignment; p. 5, Figure 2D caption; p. 32, Spectral Gap.

outcomes.name: Semantic-trajectory curvature
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The reported reference corpus contains 141 archived human animal-name sequences (PDF p. 6); n_units records that human-sequence count, not unique people or a summed human-plus-model output total. Humans generated their sequences without AI assistance; model outputs were generated separately. Average angle between consecutive semantic embedding vectors within a trajectory; higher curvature denotes sharper turns (PDF p. 33, Curvature). ConceptNet supplies the embedding space (p. 6). This is within-sequence geometry.

contrasts.reported: Human curvature 1.207, CI [1.200, 1.214]; LLM 1.066, CI [1.062, 1.071]; p < 0.0001. A numerical test statistic is not printed for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7, continuation of Cognitive Macro-Alignment; p. 5, Figure 2D caption; p. 33, Curvature.

outcomes.name: Semantic-trajectory participation ratio
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The reported reference corpus contains 141 archived human animal-name sequences (PDF p. 6); n_units records that human-sequence count, not unique people or a summed human-plus-model output total. Humans generated their sequences without AI assistance; model outputs were generated separately. Effective dimensionality of the semantic space covered by a single sequence, computed from eigenvalues of the within-trajectory ConceptNet cosine-similarity matrix (PDF pp. 32–33, Structural analysis and Participation Ratio). This measures within-sequence semantic coverage.

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 61, Figure S3C; pp. 32–33, structural-analysis definitions.

outcomes.name: Subcategory-switch fraction
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The reported reference corpus contains 141 archived human animal-name sequences (PDF p. 6); n_units records that human-sequence count, not unique people or a summed human-plus-model output total. Humans generated their sequences without AI assistance; model outputs were generated separately. Fraction of transitions that switch semantic subcategory within each sequence, defined using established category norms. Successive words are a switch when their extended Troyer/SNAFU subcategory labels do not overlap (PDF p. 25, Normative switch detection; p. 61, Figure S3B). This is a within-sequence switching fraction, not a count of distinct categories or across-person diversity.

contrasts.reported: Human M = 0.524, 95% CI [0.5067, 0.5409]; LLM M = 0.246, 95% CI [0.2350, 0.2575]; two-sided Mann–Whitney U = 223, p < 0.0001, n = 141. The benchmark count refers to source sequences, not a newly recruited AI-assistance sample.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 61, Figure S3B; p. 6, archival sequence count; p. 25, Normative switch detection.

assignment.what_was_assigned: All described participants performed the collaborative task with another human. This dataset calibrated later AI-response delays; no AI-assistance condition is described.
assignment.quote: In order to mimic human response times in the LLM-partner response times in our dyadic experiments, we collected an initial dataset from 36 human participants who performed a collaborative verbal fluency task with a human partner.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 72, Figure S13A and caption.

arms.name: Human–human timing pilot
arms.description: Human collaborative fluency responses used to fit the delay distribution for later AI partners (pp. 19, 72).

participants.who: The paper identifies an initial dataset of 36 human participants for response-time calibration; recruitment and overlap with other samples are not separately specified for this pilot (pp. 19, 72).
participants.quote: In order to mimic human response times in the LLM-partner response times in our dyadic experiments, we collected an initial dataset from 36 human participants who performed a collaborative verbal fluency task with a human partner.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 19 and 72, response-time calibration sample.

ai_tool.how_used: No AI used by these pilot participants; their response times informed subsequent artificial AI-response delays (p. 72).

task.description: Collaborative verbal fluency with a human partner in animals and clothes; response-time distributions were fitted separately by category (p. 72).

studies.label: Model-only prompt screening and response-time probes

assignment.what_was_assigned: Prompt conditions were applied to simulated LLM partners, not assigned to people. A separate temporal probe varied the response-time value in a model prompt.
assignment.quote: in which one (primary) LLM is playing the role of the human partner and the other (secondary) LLM is given the range of prompts to test.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 67, Figure S8; p. 64, Figure S6.

arms.name: Solo LLM
arms.description: Model generates category words alone from a human-derived seed (p. 67).

arms.name: LLM–LLM default
arms.description: Secondary model receives the primary model’s prompt (p. 67).

arms.name: LLM–LLM convergent
arms.description: Secondary model is prompted to generate a nearby semantic item (p. 67).

arms.name: LLM–LLM divergent
arms.description: Secondary model is prompted to generate a distant semantic item (p. 67).

arms.name: LLM–LLM inferred
arms.description: Secondary model chooses a nearby or distant item intended to help its partner (p. 67).

arms.name: LLM temporal-context probe
arms.description: Model is prompted with different hypothetical response times while predicting a continuation (p. 64).

participants.who: Model-only analyses: human archival sequences supplied contexts, not recruited human intervention participants. Dyadic simulations used seeds from 699 human sequences; the temporal probe used 50 distinct human sequences (pp. 64, 67).
participants.quote: in which one (primary) LLM is playing the role of the human partner and the other (secondary) LLM is given the range of prompts to test.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 64 and 67, Figures S6 and S8.

ai_tool.name_model: LLM model identifier not stated in the simulation caption; Gemini-2.5-Flash for the temporal probe
ai_tool.how_used: Two LLMs alternated category words under different prompting strategies and were compared with solo generation; the temporal probe separately tested model continuations under different stated retrieval times (pp. 64, 67).

task.description: Simulated animal-name semantic fluency, scoring semantic distance through the generated sequence; separate temporal-context prediction probe (pp. 64, 67).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Archived human datasets are reused from Hills, Jones, and Todd (2012), Optimal foraging in semantic memory, and Zemla, Gooding, and Austerweil (2023), Evidence for optimal semantic search throughout adulthood. These are existing datasets, not new independent human samples (PDF pp. 6, 10 and 31; Supplementary References [14]–[15], pp. 76–77). Within this paper, solo sequences from Experiments 1 and 3 are pooled for later comparisons (p. 29). No further cross-paper participant overlap is stated for the newly recruited collaboration sample.

eligibility.reason: Experiment 4 remains unresolved for core inclusion: AI prompt type varied between participants and partner type within participants, with partner order and category counterbalanced, but random assignment of AI prompts or condition order is not stated (PDF p. 30, Experiment 4). Counterbalancing establishes neither randomized nor non-random allocation, so design_class remains other and criterion 1 remains unclear. The explicitly reported 129 people in paired analyses meet the people threshold (p. 71, Figure S12). The full condition samples contain 192 people in human–human dyads and 144 in human–AI dyads, with overlapping participants; these counts must not be summed (pp. 11 and 30). Individual and dyadic unique-concept counts and computed semantic relations are scored on produced words, meeting the output criterion (pp. 11–14 and 70–75). Randomization in Experiments 2 and 3 concerns sequence stimuli, not AI assistance (p. 29). Separately, the comparison of independently model-generated sequences with archived unassisted human sequences qualifies as ai_vs_human context (p. 6, Cognitive Macro-Alignment); this paper-level context classification does not resolve the collaboration experiment’s assignment.

one_line_finding: AI partners did not increase individual human concept production compared with human partners (U = 1.45 × 10^4, p = 0.44; PDF p. 14, Figure 5D), and random assignment of AI assistance or condition order was not stated (p. 30).
